Reproachfully
rē-prōch´fool-lē
adv. (with reproach; in a manner conveying contempt)
From reproach, Old French reprocher, to cast back in one's teeth. It occurs twice: of Job's tormentors, and of the occasion a careless household gives an adversary.

Biblical Definition

Job describes what his comforters have become: “They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me” (Job 16:10). The blow to the cheek is contempt made physical, and the word marks the manner rather than the injury. Paul uses the adverb in a directive about household order: “I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully” (1 Timothy 5:14). The concern is the mouth of an opponent, and the apostle assumes that conduct in a Christian home is being watched and will be spoken of. He states the same principle for servants: “Let as many servants as are under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed” (1 Timothy 6:1). And Peter grounds the whole concern in what God does with such conduct: “Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:12). Reproach against the church, when it is deserved, falls on the doctrine and on the Name.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines reproach as censure mingled with contempt or derision; and reproachfully as in a manner conveying reproach or contempt.

expand to see more

REPROACH, v.t. To censure with severity, or with contemptuous language; to upbraid.

REPROACHFULLY, adv. In terms of reproach; opprobriously; with contempt; shamefully.

ADVERSARY, n. An enemy or foe; one who opposes another in a suit at law.

BLASPHEME, v.t. To speak of the Supreme Being in terms of impious irreverence; to revile or speak reproachfully of God.

CONVERSATION, n. In Scripture, general course of manners; behavior; deportment.

Key Scripture

Job 16:10 — "They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me."

1 Timothy 5:14 — "I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully."

1 Timothy 6:1 — "Let as many servants as are under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed."

1 Peter 2:12 — "Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation."

Modern Corruption

Concern for the church's reputation is dismissed as people-pleasing, or else inflated until avoiding criticism becomes the governing rule of Christian conduct.

expand to see more

One error treats Paul's concern about giving the adversary occasion as mere respectability — a first-century preoccupation with appearances that a bolder faith would shrug off. The apostles do not shrug it off. They tie the church's conduct directly to whether the name of God and His doctrine are blasphemed, which makes it a matter of the third commandment rather than of public relations. What outsiders say about a household or a congregation attaches, in Scripture's reckoning, to the God whose name it bears.

The opposite error makes the avoidance of reproach into the supreme rule, so that whatever the world finds offensive is quietly dropped. That is not what Paul asks. He asks for conduct that gives no occasion — that is, that the reproach, when it comes, should be a lie. Peter assumes it will come anyway: they speak against you as evildoers. Christ promised as much. The distinction the church must keep is between reproach earned by sin, which dishonours God, and reproach earned by fidelity, which Scripture calls blessed. Job's tormentors smote him reproachfully, and God said at the end that Job had spoken rightly.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew cherpah (H2781), reproach, disgrace; Greek loidoria (G3059), reviling; antikeimenos (G480), the adversary; blasphemeo (G987), to speak evil of.

expand to see more

Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, scorn; the manner of the blow in Job 16:10.

Greek loidoria (G3059) — reviling, abuse; occasion to speak reproachfully, 1 Timothy 5:14.

Greek antikeimai (G480) — to be an adversary, to oppose; the one watching the household.

Greek blasphemeo (G987) — to revile, speak injuriously; of God's name and doctrine.

Greek anastrophe (G391) — manner of life, conversation; 1 Peter 2:12.

Usage

"“They have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully” — contempt made physical."

"“Give none occasion to the adversary” — the apostolic charge to households."

"“That the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed” — what is at stake."
